articles.title: La placa tectónica de Oceanía es la más rápida de la Tierra, desplazándose siete centímetros cada año, casi el doble de rápido de lo que crecen las uñas
articles.standfirst: El movimiento es imperceptible para quienes estén en su superficie
articles.summary: El movimiento es imperceptible para quienes estén en su superficie
articles.body: Australia se mueve. Y lo hace a un ritmo que, aunque imperceptible para cualquiera que esté sobre su superficie, resulta sorprendentemente rápido a escala geológica: unos siete centímetros cada año hacia el noreste. Es suficiente para convertirla en la masa continental que más rápido se desplaza sobre la Tierra. La cifra adquiere una dimensión más fácil de entender si se compara con algo cotidiano, con una acción a la que estamos totalmente acostumbrados. Un estudio calculó que las uñas crecen, de media, unos 3,47 milímetros al mes, alrededor de 4,2 centímetros al año. Es decir, Australia avanza aproximadamente 1,7 veces más rápido que una uña humana, apunta el medio de comunicación Science Blog. La velocidad tampoco significa que Australia sea la placa tectónica más rápida del planeta en términos absolutos. Existen zonas de placas oceánicas que superan los diez centímetros anuales. La particularidad australiana es que se trata de la masa continental que se desplaza más deprisa. Y ese movimiento tiene consecuencias prácticas. Australia ha tenido que actualizar sus sistemas de coordenadas porque el continente continúa desplazándose mientras los mapas permanecen estáticos. El antiguo sistema nacional de referencia fijaba las posiciones tomando como referencia la situación del territorio en 1994. Para 2020, la diferencia respecto a un marco global moderno había alcanzado aproximadamente 1,8 metros. La precisión es especialmente importante ahora que tecnologías como la agricultura de precisión, la topografía, la construcción o los sistemas de navegación trabajan con posicionamientos de centímetros. A una escala mucho mayor, el desplazamiento también está cambiando la posición de Australia respecto al resto del planeta. Durante millones de años se ha alejado de la Antártida y se ha acercado a la zona de Indonesia y Nueva Guinea. Algunos modelos geodinámicos incluso plantean que, dentro de 200 o 300 millones de años, Australia podría formar parte de un nuevo supercontinente. Pero esa última posibilidad es una predicción a una escala temporal enorme. Lo que sí sabemos es que Australia ya se está moviendo (siete centímetros cada año), y que la Tierra cambia mucho más de lo que aparentan sus mapas.

articles.title: In 2010, Thailand sank 25 retired battle tanks into the Gulf to rebuild fishing grounds; 9 years later, researchers found 53 fish species
articles.summary: Science News: Battle tank is made for war. It is built to cross tough terrain, take a beating and dominate a battlefield. But what if the battlefield disappears and.
articles.body: Battle tank is made for war. It is built to cross tough terrain, take a beating and dominate a battlefield. But what if the battlefield disappears and there is no place for the tank to go? Some retired tanks have found an unexpectedly useful second life, under the sea in southern Thailand. According to an online repor by Aljazeera, in August 2010 Thailand’s army sank 25 old Chinese-made battle tanks into the Gulf of Thailand off Narathiwat province. 273 old railroad cars and 198 scrapped garbage trucks went under the water to serve as an artificial reef and create new fishing grounds. The strange undersea haul was part of an effort to help fishing communities whose catches have plummeted after decades of overfishing. And then, over the next few years, something astonishing happened: the cast-off military hardware began to attract marine life.As per the report, it all began with a problem common to fishing communities around the world. Local fishermen in southern Thailand had complained of dwindling catches and finally appealed to Queen Sirikit for help. The response included an unusual thought, why not not just dump old equipment, but put it to work under the waves? The tanks were particularly well designed for the purpose, since they had already become obsolete. According to Bangkok Post reporting, Thailand bought them second-hand from China in 1987 at a discounted price and they were decommissioned in 2004. They were essentially steel not used by the army. But for the fishing industry, they could be something else entirely. The 2010 sinking, Al Jazeera reported, left the tanks next to hundreds of old railroad cars and scrapped garbage trucks. Collectively, the structures would supply the hard surfaces and shelter that a sandy seafloor cannot.What did they put in the tanks?Almost 10 years after the tanks went under, researchers from Ramkhamhaeng University in Bangkok did some diving to see what had grown up around the man-made reef sites. Their study “First Insight on the Fish Species Composition at Two Artificial Reef Areas, Narathiwat Province, Thailand” listed 53 fish species of 21 families that live around the tanks and the nearby sunken railroad wagons. Snappers were the most diverse group with seven species recorded. Then four species each of damselfish and wrasses. Also, the scientists found an interesting difference between the structures. The closed-in tanks held much larger schools of fish than the more open railroad wagons. Species recorded included commercially important fish such as snappers and the critically endangered humphead parrotfish. What had once been military hardware now offered shelter and feeding grounds and habitat for an underwater community.Why does a steel tank act like a reef?A reef does not necessarily have to look like coral to a fish. It’s the structure that’s important for what it provides. The flat, sandy seafloor provides relatively little for many reef-associated species. Vertical surfaces, crevices and sheltered spaces are created by a submerged tank, train car or other solid structure. As time goes by, algae, barnacles and other organisms colonize those surfaces. These tiny beasts then become food for smaller fish. The smaller fish attract bigger predators An abandoned piece of infrastructure can gradually become the basis for an entire food web. That is the simple idea behind artificial reefs. According to the report, this is not a practice unique to Thailand. Countries such as Japan, the United States and India have tried to create habitat and improve fishing grounds by using artificial structures built from boats, railroad materials, concrete and other durable materials.Figures suggest artificial reefs can pay offThe Narathiwat project seems to support local assertions that artificial reefs can improve fishing opportunities, but no independent study has quantified the increase in catches specifically around the Narathiwat tank reefs. But there is some interesting evidence elsewhere in the research. H. Mohamad Kasim and colleagues from India’s Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute published a study on the economic performance of artificial reefs along the Tamil Nadu coast in southern India in the Indian Journal of Fisheries in 2013. They found that fish catches per unit of fishing effort were 34% higher in reef areas compared to open fishing zones. Gillnet fisherman had a net income nearly three times greater near the artificial reefs. The scientists also discovered that the cost of building the reefs could be recouped in around two and a half months. But those results don't show that Thailand's tanks produced the same economic benefits. But they show why artificial reefs have become of interest as a tool to help fishing communities.Artificial reefs are not a magic bulletBut there is an important question behind the success stories. Are artificial reefs really increasing fish populations, or are they simply aggregating fish from elsewhere? The argument is not conclusively settled among scientists. An artificial reef that merely concentrates fish from a large area into a convenient location can look like a great success at first glance. Fishermen would catch more fish around the reef, but the overall population might not have grown. And that concentration could cause a new problem: overfishing. A popular artificial reef can be an easy target for fishermen and may deplete the very population it is intended to support. This is why successful artificial-reef programs often have fishing regulations such as catch limits or other restrictions to allow fish populations to reproduce. The performance of the reef can also depend on many environmental factors like depth, strength and direction of currents, materials used to build the reef and shape of the reef itself. Those variables might help explain why some artificial reefs become thriving ecosystems while others yield more modest results.A broader reef-building experimentThe tanks were not an isolated experiment. By 2008, Thailand's broader artificial-reef program in the region had already expanded to include donated railroad materials and concrete pipes supplied by government departments, including the state railway and highways authorities. The 2010 sinking of the tanks simply became its most striking and widely reported chapter. There is something almost poetic about the transformation. Objects designed to occupy battlefields were placed on the seabed and given an entirely different purpose.

articles.title: Scientists found an estimated 5.5 million wild bees beneath just 1.5 acres of a New York cemetery, more than three times Manhattan's human population
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Beneath the quiet lawns and weathered headstones of a small cemetery in Ithaca, New York, scientists have uncovered one of the most astonishing bee di.
articles.body: Beneath the quiet lawns and weathered headstones of a small cemetery in Ithaca, New York, scientists have uncovered one of the most astonishing bee discoveries in recent memory. In a carefully studied 1.5-acre section of the cemetery grounds, researchers estimated that about 5.5 million wild, ground-nesting bees live in a dense network of underground nests. That number is more than three times the entire human population of Manhattan, packed into an area smaller than many city blocks. As reported by Cornell University and ScienceDaily, the finding highlights how urban and suburban landscapes can harbour vast, hidden reservoirs of biodiversity, and it challenges common assumptions about where nature thrives in a developed world.A cemetery that hums with lifeTo the casual visitor, the cemetery looks like many others in the Northeast. Grass is mowed in neat rows. Trees shade winding paths. Gravestones stand in orderly lines. But in late spring and early summer, the ground in certain sections comes alive in a different way. Tiny holes dot the soil, each one the entrance to a bee nest. From these openings, thousands of small, dark bees emerge and return in a constant, low hum.The bees are ground-nesting species, meaning they dig their nests into bare or sparsely vegetated soil rather than building hives in trees or man-made structures. Many people associate bees with honey-producing colonies in wooden boxes, but the majority of wild bee species are solitary or live in small family groups, and a large share of them nest in the ground. The cemetery, with its open, well-drained lawns and limited pesticide use, turns out to be an ideal place for them to raise their young.How researchers counted the uncountableCounting millions of tiny, fast-moving insects is not a simple task. The research team, led by scientists from Cornell University, used a combination of field surveys, statistical modelling and extrapolation to arrive at their estimate. They began by mapping the areas of the cemetery in which bee nests were concentrated, and within those areas, they estimated nest density by counting the number of nest entrances in sample plots of known size. They then factored in data on how many female bees typically occupy a single nest and how many offspring each female produces over a nesting season. By combining nest density, nest occupancy and reproductive rates, they were able to estimate the total number of individual bees using the 1.5-acre study area over the course of a season. The result, about 5.5 million bees, is an estimate rather than an exact count, but it is grounded in rigorous sampling and peer-reviewed methods.Why so many bees in such a small spaceSeveral features of the cemetery make it unusually favourable for ground-nesting bees. The soil is well drained and relatively compact, which helps nests stay stable and dry. Regular mowing keeps the vegetation short and creates patches of bare ground that many of the bee species prefer for nesting. At the same time, the surrounding landscape provides a steady supply of flowers, from early spring blooms to late summer wildflowers, so that adult bees have enough nectar and pollen to feed themselves and their larvae. Importantly, the cemetery is managed with minimal pesticide use. Many urban and suburban lawns are treated with insecticides and herbicides that can kill bees directly or reduce the availability of flowering plants. In this cemetery, the management approach prioritises long term landscape stability and low chemical inputs, creating a safer environment for nesting insects.The result is a place where bees can reproduce in extraordinary numbers without conflicting heavily with human activities. Visitors may notice the bees, especially on warm, sunny days, but the insects are generally non-aggressive and focused on foraging and nest building rather than defending a large communal hive.The finding in the Ithaca cemetery has gotten attention because it flies in the face of common stories about where wildlife can find refuge in human-made landscapes. Cities and towns are often thought to be inhospitable to native bees, which are thought to require large swaths of natural habitat to thrive.This study shows that even small, seemingly mundane patches of green space can support massive populations if they are managed in a bee-friendly way. Cemeteries, parks, school grounds and other open spaces are scattered throughout urban areas. If managed with nesting habitat and floral resources in mind, they could function as a network of refuges for wild bees. The sheer number of bees found in just 1.5 acres implies that the total bee biomass in such landscapes could be far larger than previously recognised.For conservationists, the takeaway is not that all cemeteries should be left unmanaged, but that modest changes in mowing schedules, pesticide policies and soil disturbance can make a big difference. Leaving some areas of bare ground, reducing chemical inputs and planting native flowering species can turn ordinary lawns into productive bee habitat.Importance of ground-nesting bees to ecosystemsGround-nesting bees are important pollinators. Many are generalist foragers, visiting a wide range of wildflowers, garden plants and crops. Some are specialists, only visiting a few plant species within a family, forging close ecological links that support plant diversity. They tend to forage near their nests and thus provide very localised pollination services to plants near their colonies.Most ground-nesting bees are solitary or live in small groups, unlike honey bees that are social and live in large perennial colonies. Females construct and provision their own nests, laying eggs in individual cells provisioned with pollen and nectar. This life history renders them especially susceptible to disruptions at the nest site, such as frequent tilling, high foot traffic or pesticide use that contaminates the soil.The presence of millions of these bees in a single site underscores how critical undisturbed ground is to their survival, as well as the potential for human-managed landscapes to support not just a few isolated nests but entire population strongholds.Implications for bee conservation and land managementThe Ithaca study comes at a time when wild bee populations are threatened by habitat loss, pesticide exposure, disease and climate change. Many conservation efforts focus on planting pollinator gardens or installing bee hotels, which may help some species but do not meet the needs of ground nesters. This research suggests that protecting and creating suitable nesting substrate is equally important. Land managers in urban and suburban areas can take several lessons from the cemetery example. Reducing the frequency and intensity of soil disturbance, limiting pesticide use and maintaining a mosaic of mowed and unmowed areas can all support ground-nesting bees. Even small adjustments, such as leaving some patches of bare soil along edges or under trees, can provide nesting opportunities.At the policy level, the findings encourage a broader view of green infrastructure. Cemeteries, utility corridors, roadside verges and other overlooked spaces could be incorporated into pollinator conservation plans, not just as sources of flowers but as nesting habitat. Recognising that millions of bees can live beneath our feet in places we walk every day may help shift public perception of what counts as valuable nature.A quiet miracle beneath the gravestonesFor the researchers walking among the headstones, the project was as humbling as it was fascinating. A vibrant, hidden world had been thriving underfoot the entire time, completely unnoticed.Finding 5.5 million bees living beneath just 1.5 acres of cemetery grass isn't a problem to solve; it is proof that nature can flourish inside manicured human spaces. It also points to a huge, untapped opportunity for towns everywhere. If a quiet cemetery in upstate New York can support a population that size, rethinking how we manage our everyday parks, yards, and lawns could easily give these underground communities room to thrive.

articles.title: Southern California anglers are catching unusually large fish rarely seen this far north as Pacific waters warm
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Southern California anglers are seeing an unusual number of warm-water fish as rising ocean temperatures linked to El Niño and marine heatwaves bring .
articles.body: Southern California anglers are seeing an unusual number of warm-water fish as rising ocean temperatures linked to El Niño and marine heatwaves bring species typically found farther south into local waters.Fishermen working in Marina del Rey and Santa Monica are catching fish species, in larger sizes, that are rarely seen in the area. Tony Villanueva, a boat captain who has been operating out of the area for years, describes the haul as unprecedented.“Biggest yellowtail I've ever seen up here,” Villanueva told ABC 7.Another captain, Alex Garcia, also said that anglers have been getting unusually large catches. “We've been catching a bunch of big bonito,” Garcia said.These species of fish are often seen in waters off Mexico, but now they are appearing along the Southern California coast.“People go on overnight trips and pay big money to go catch the fish that we're catching right here, right in our backyard,” Garcia added.Ocean temperatures off Southern California have risen well above normal due to a marine heatwave overlapping with El Niño conditions. Dr Julia Coates, an environmental scientist with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, told the broadcaster that warmer ocean conditions are driving these changes.“Right now we're experiencing warm water due to what's called a marine heatwave,” the scientist told the outlet.She explained that the marine heatwave is bringing unusually warm water to Southern California, drawing tropical and pelagic species that typically inhabit deeper waters. These unusual conditions have resulted in these rare sightings for local anglers. “To see a hammerhead shark with yellowtails swimming around it was pretty cool.”Boat captains who have spent decades fishing in the local waters have called it a rare event.“We had fish up to, like, 25, almost pushing 30 pounds. Unheard of here, unheard of. Dorado, catching dorado on the anchor right off Santa Monica,” Villanueva said.Garcia observed that water temperatures are significantly higher than normal. “The water temperature obviously is way higher than it usually is. It's like 76 degrees out there.”The temporary abundance is exciting; however, it may upend local fishing economics. Coates added that warmer waters have boosted fishing opportunities; similar conditions in the past have had serious environmental consequences. “We saw a dramatic loss of kelp and kelp forests in Northern CA, that ecosystem was dramatically changed and has not yet recovered,” Coates explained, referring to the previous thermal anomaly.Villanueva also commented on the effects of unusually warm water farther south. “Down south, the water's so warm that it's actually killing off some fish because the water's too warm.”Coates also cautioned against viewing the fish boom as simple good fortune. Between 2013 and 2016, Southern California experienced a similar collision of El Niño and extended marine heatwaves during an event called ‘The Blob’. Local fishing operators have plans to continue running trips despite expectations for high surf. “The fish are out there, it's a really cool time to get out on the water,” Garcia said.

articles.title: Scientists discovered an underwater city of 20,000 octopus nests deep inside California coast; largest known nursery on the planet
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Researchers have located the planet's largest known octopus nursery deep off the Californian coast, documenting 5,718 animals in 2.5 hectares and esti.
articles.body: Researchers have located the planet's largest known octopus nursery deep off the Californian coast, documenting 5,718 animals in 2.5 hectares and estimating about 20,000 around Davidson Seamount. Known as the Octopus Garden, the nursery is located about 10,500 feet below the surface off Central California. According to a statement released by the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) on August 23, 2023, monitoring confirmed that pearl octopuses migrate to the site for mating and nesting.The Octopus GardenThe nursery is situated on a small hill near the base of the Davidson Seamount, which is an extinct volcano located 130 kilometres southwest of Monterey, California. The large concentration first drew attention in October 2018. Researchers from the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, NOAA, Ocean Exploration Trust, and collaborators, working aboard the E/V Nautilus, observed thousands of octopuses gathered on a rocky rise near the seamount.The position of the animals helped researchers understand exactly what was happening in the section of the ocean. Many of the octopuses were upside down, with their arms positioned around their bodies, a posture that is associated with females protecting and incubating their eggs.The species was identified as Muusoctopus robustus, known to researchers as the pearl octopus. They exhibit a pale purple colouration. According to MBARI, the animal is approximately the size of a grapefruit and occurs in the northeastern Pacific Ocean, from Oregon down to Baja California. The institute has observed the species at depths between 2,300 and 3,600 metres.Research on the nurseryAfter the initial discovery, researchers began a prolonged investigation to determine why so many animals were concentrated at that point. For three years, the institute and its partner institutions employed cameras, sensors, remotely operated vehicles and other equipment to observe the behaviour of octopuses and the environmental conditions of the nursery.Doc Ricketts, a remotely operated vehicle from MBARI, played a central role in the research. The team conducted 14 dives with the ROV during which scientists found adult males and females, developing eggs and hatchlings. No individuals of intermediate size or evidence of feeding were observed at the site. These observations indicated that the octopuses gather there specifically to mate and nest. The size of the concentration was measured using a combination of photographs and detailed mapping of the seabed. The LASS system, installed on the Doc Ricketts ROV, allowed high-resolution images to be produced and a photomosaic of the region to be assembled. In this survey, researchers documented 5,718 octopuses in just 2.5 hectares at the centre of the Octopus Garden. The slight elevation where the nursery is located occupies approximately 333 hectares, or 823 acres. Based on the surveys conducted, the team calculated that the total population could easily exceed 20,000 individuals.It is the thermal conditions of the area that explain why this small area attracts so many animals. At approximately 3,200 meters, the normal water temperature is around 1.6°C. However, in the crevices and fissures used by the octopuses, water warmed by the hydrothermal vents reaches nearly 11°C. The initial researchers observed a "sparkling" appearance in the water, caused by the mixture of hot and cold water. Subsequent investigations confirmed the existence of hydrothermal vents and showed that the nests are clustered precisely in the fissures bathed by the warmer water emerging from the seabed.Why this region?Octopuses are ectothermic animals, and the cold deep waters reduce their metabolism and slow embryonic development. At temperatures close to zero found in the abyssal environment, researchers expected that the pearl octopus's eggs would need five to eight years or even longer to hatch.But the temperature in these locations revealed a different outcome. Using 4K imaging and features like scars to recognise the animals, scientists tracked their clutches and found that the eggs hatched in less than two years. This acceleration was attributed to the heat from he hydrothermal vents, which increases the mothers' and embryos' metabolism. The longer the incubation, the greater the period during which the embryos are subject to predation, injury, infections, and other sources of mortality.Females migrate to the Octopus Garden in search of warm locations where they can nest. Each one lays a clutch of approximately 60 elongated eggs and covers the embryos with her body while they develop.Interestingly, the nursery also serves as a food source for other species. As is typically the case with cephalopods, both male and female pearl octopuses die after reproduction. Most mother remain alive until the eggs hatch, though some exhaust their reserves before development is complete. Their carcasses are consumed by various organisms from the area. Ratfish, cusk eels, sea slugs, anemones, and other scavengers take advantage of the remains left after reproduction. Researchers estimated that this biomass provides 72% more food to the local marine community than would be available outside the Octopus Garden.The Octopus Garden is described by MBARI as the largest known concentration of octopuses on the planet to date.

articles.title: Scientists removed more than 70% of underwater logs from one half of a Wisconsin lake; within 2 years its once-dominant yellow perch population had nearly disappeared
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: From the surface a lake might look like it is not changing at all but underneath it is a very different story. Scientists demonstrated how important f.
articles.body: From the surface a lake might look like it is not changing at all but underneath it is a very different story. Scientists demonstrated how important fallen trees and submerged logs can be to freshwater ecosystems in an unusual whole-lake experiment under calm waters of Wisconsin’s Little Rock Lake. In the study, ‘The rapid effects of a whole-lake reduction of coarse woody debris on fish and benthic macroinvertebrates’, researchers removed over 70% of the coarse woody habitat from one basin of the lake, and the effects were quickly seen in its fish. Yellow perch, which was once the lake’s most abundant fish, plummeted to very low numbers within two years, the study adds. The study was conducted in Little Rock Lake, an 18-hectare undeveloped, unfished lake in Vilas County, Wisconsin. A large curtain divides the lake into 2 similar basins. Fish and water cannot pass between the basins. That unusual setup gave researchers a natural laboratory setting. One basin was designated as the treatment area in which approximately 70% of the coarse woody debris along the shallow shore was removed in 2002. The other basin was left as a control. The aim was to determine what happens when a key feature of the habitat is removed.Why underwater logs are importantFallen trees and branches might appear to be nothing more than debris but they create complex underwater environments. Logs provide fish with places to hide, feed and shelter and also increase the variety of habitat available in the lake. The two basins had broadly similar food webs dominated by aquatic prey before the experiment. But after removal of the woody habitat, the fish community started to respond differently.Decline of yellow perchThe most striking change was the decline in yellow perch, which had been the most abundant fish species in the lake. Perch densities in the treatment basin dropped to very low levels. Researchers attributed the decline to increased predation and little or no successful recruitment of young fish. It was a stark contrast to the pristine basin. In the reference basin, yellow perch produced several generations of young in successive years, thus rebuilding the population. Thus, woody cover loss appeared to influence where fish were found and their ability to survive and maintain populations.Bass altered their behaviorLargemouth bass also responded to the changed habitat. After log removal, bass in the treatment basin consumed less fish and relied more on terrestrial prey. Their growth also slowed relative to bass in the reference basin. The results suggest that removing underwater structure can alter predator-prey relationships across an entire ecosystem, not just impact a single species in isolation.Not every species responded immediatelyOddly the experiment did not produce the same rapid changes in aquatic invertebrates. There was no significant difference in the composition, diversity or density of benthic macroinvertebrate communities between the treatment and reference basins during the two years following the habitat reduction. That contrast illustrates how different parts of an ecosystem can respond at very different speeds.A warning for developed coastsThe findings have implications beyond Little Rock Lake. As shorelines are developed, riparian forests may be thinned and fallen trees removed from shallow water for esthetic or recreational reasons. The experiment shows that such small changes can have big implications for fish communities. The study, Fish Community and Food Web Responses to a Whole-Lake Removal of Coarse Woody Habitat, shows that keeping submerged woody habitat is important to support desirable fish populations and healthy fisheries. What looks like clutter from above may be, below the surface, critical infrastructure for an entire aquatic food web.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia
